To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the ERCC1 gene is a member of the XPF family of DNA repair genes; (2) the ERCC3 gene is the human homolog of the yeast rad2 gene; and (3) the ERCC4 gene is the human RAD16 homolog.

(1) the Ercc1 coding sequence is 3,000 bp in length, and contains 12 exons; (2) the ERCC1 protein contains 2 domains, an N-terminal domain and a C-terminal domain; and (3) the C-terminal domain contains a region that interacts with the XPB helicase.

we isolated and characterized the Ercc1 coding sequence from 10 ERCC mutant Chinese hamster ovay (CHO) cell lines and found two general classes of mutations, including nucleotide additions or delentions that produced frameshift mutations and point mutations that resulted transitions and transversions, including non-sense mutations and mutations that generate intron/exon errors, and that the relative level of Ercc1 protein differed significantly both among parental cell lines and mutant cell lines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of Chinese hamster cell mutants defective in the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway, and in particular with the characterization of the ERCC1 locus.
the molecular characterization and functional analysis of Chinese hamaster ovary ERCC1 mutant genes.
the characterization of ERCC1 mutant CHO cell lines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the CHO-ERCC1 gene encodes a protein that is involved in nucleotide excision repair of DNA and that mutations in this gene can be divided into two classes: (1) mutations that result in a loss of function and (2) mutations that result primarily in a reduction in Ercc protein levels.
the ERCC1 gene is composed of a minimum of 11 exons and is located on the X chromosome between the Xp22.2 and Xp11.4 regions.
ERCC1 is a complex gene, with multiple mutations that can be isolated in CHO cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CHO ERCC1 mutant genes fall into at least four complementation groups, and that the mutations in these genes may result in either a complete loss of Ercc1 protein, or in the production of Ercc1 proteins with altered properties.
the ERCC1 protein is required for both nucleotide excision repair and transcription-coupled repair.

the mutations we identified in the Ercc1 gene of CHO mutant cell lines are consistent with the hypothesis that Ercc1 plays a role in nucleotide excision repair and that the mutations are responsible for the ERCC1 phenotype of these mutant cell lines.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the ERCC1 protein is a very unstable protein and that the majority of the mutations that we have observed in the ERCC1 gene are not in the XPA binding domain but in the N-terminal region of the protein.
the CHO Ercc1 gene is a complex gene that contains a variety of mutations that can result in a spectrum of phenotypes.
ERCC1 mutants are not all the same and that the mutations that are found in the ERCC1 gene can be used to predict the phenotype and the complementation group of the mutant.
